Les Orcs sont généralement présentés par Tolkien comme des êtres cruels, querelleurs et prompts à exploiter la faiblesse d'autrui. Ces comportements sont profondément enracinés dans leur histoire, puisque des générations ont vécu dans des sociétés où la domination, le châtiment et la violence constituent les principaux moyens de faire respecter l'autorité. La peur joue un rôle essentiel dans ces relations. Un soldat obéit à un capitaine qu'il déteste parce qu'il connaît les conséquences d'un refus, un artisan accepte des exigences excessives pour conserver son atelier et un éclaireur dissimule une erreur lorsqu'il sait que son supérieur chercherait à en faire un exemple. Cette crainte entretient la méfiance entre individus, particulièrement lorsque la dénonciation d'un compagnon permet d'obtenir une récompense ou qu'un chef encourage les rivalités afin de prévenir les complots contre son autorité.

Certains Orcs participent volontiers à cette violence et cherchent à accroître leur puissance, tandis que d'autres s'y conforment parce qu'ils n'ont jamais connu d'autre organisation ou redoutent de devenir eux-mêmes les victimes de leurs compagnons. Les récits montrent cependant qu'ils peuvent éprouver des désirs personnels distincts des ambitions de leurs maîtres. Certains souhaitent conserver une part du butin, quitter une garnison ou vivre dans une région éloignée des grandes guerres. Cette volonté de s'affranchir des ordres ne s'accompagne pas nécessairement du désir de renoncer aux habitudes brutales acquises au cours de leur existence. Un Orc qui déserte les armées de Sauron peut rechercher simplement sa propre sécurité, souhaiter prendre le commandement d'une bande ou s'emparer d'un territoire dont il entend contrôler les ressources.

La question de leur responsabilité individuelle demeure délicate dans l'univers de Tolkien, qui continua lui-même de réfléchir à la nature morale des Orcs et aux conséquences de leur origine. Il convient donc de préserver deux dimensions essentielles : leur existence fut profondément façonnée par la domination de l'Ombre, mais leurs actes et leurs décisions ne doivent pas être présentés comme de simples mouvements dépourvus de toute volonté. Un personnage peut demeurer cruel, poursuivre des ambitions personnelles ou chercher à reproduire les rapports de force qu'il a toujours connus. Il peut également, dans le cadre d'une campagne, être confronté à des circonstances qui l'amènent à remettre en question certaines habitudes. Une telle évolution exige des expériences, des décisions et des conséquences réelles, particulièrement lorsque le personnage doit apprendre à comprendre des relations fondées sur la confiance plutôt que sur la peur.

Incarner un Orc

Jouer un Orc en Terre du Milieu, c'est incarner un personnage dont l'existence est profondément marquée par une société hostile, des rapports de pouvoir dangereux et un héritage associé aux puissances de l'Ombre. Sa constitution lui accorde des qualités physiques remarquables, mais son éducation détermine les connaissances qu'il possède réellement et les comportements qu'il a appris. Un jeune Orc peut avoir grandi dans les galeries des Monts Brumeux, où il connaît les passages de sa communauté, les chemins empruntés par les patrouilles et les endroits où trouver les ressources nécessaires à la subsistance de sa bande. Il a appris à obéir aux chefs, à reconnaître leurs rivalités et à conserver ses possessions à l'abri des individus plus puissants. Son départ peut résulter d'une querelle, de la disparition du capitaine qui le protégeait ou d'une expédition dont il fut le seul survivant. Il peut également avoir reçu une mission de reconnaissance dans une région éloignée et découvert, après un événement imprévu, que son retour présenterait davantage de dangers que la poursuite de son voyage.

Un autre personnage peut appartenir aux garnisons du Mordor, où il a reçu une formation militaire et appris les signaux employés dans les forteresses. Ses supérieurs attendent de lui une obéissance stricte, particulièrement lorsqu'il doit surveiller un passage, accompagner un convoi ou participer à une opération contre les ennemis de Sauron. Une désertion devient alors une entreprise particulièrement périlleuse, puisqu'il doit échapper à la surveillance de ses anciens compagnons et éviter les routes fréquentées par les troupes de son maître. Il peut connaître les pratiques militaires des armées de l'Ombre et posséder des renseignements précieux sur leurs fortifications, mais leur divulgation risque également de le désigner comme un traître aux yeux des autres Orcs. Son existence dépend alors de sa capacité à trouver une région où il pourra survivre, particulièrement lorsque son apparence lui ferme la plupart des refuges disponibles auprès des Peuples Libres.

Un artisan orc possède une expérience différente. Il a passé de longues années dans une forge, un atelier de cuir ou un établissement chargé d'entretenir des machines militaires. Il connaît les métaux, les mécanismes et les objets récupérés au cours des raids, tandis que son travail lui donne une utilité reconnue par les chefs de sa communauté. Cette compétence peut le protéger de certaines violences, mais l'expose également aux exigences de supérieurs qui attendent des résultats immédiats et disposent du pouvoir de le dépouiller de ses outils. Son départ peut être provoqué par un conflit avec un capitaine, la recherche de matériaux difficiles à obtenir ou le désir de conserver un objet que son supérieur entend s'approprier. Il peut également souhaiter offrir ses services à une autre bande, particulièrement lorsqu'il estime que ses connaissances lui permettront d'obtenir une position plus favorable.

Un éclaireur peut posséder une connaissance approfondie d'un territoire, particulièrement lorsqu'il a passé plusieurs années à rechercher des passages, à surveiller les caravanes et à observer les mouvements des populations voisines. Il sait reconnaître les signes laissés par une troupe, retrouver un chemin praticable pendant la nuit et choisir un endroit favorable à une embuscade. Ces compétences peuvent lui permettre de survivre loin de sa communauté, mais elles l'exposent également aux dangers des régions traversées. Une Orque issue d'un établissement souterrain peut avoir appris à gérer les réserves, entretenir les équipements ou organiser certaines activités nécessaires à la vie collective. Selon les développements retenus par le Meneur, son éducation peut comprendre la chasse, les métiers artisanaux ou les techniques de défense de sa communauté. La rareté des informations concernant les femmes orques chez Tolkien laisse une place à l'interprétation, dont les détails doivent demeurer cohérents avec les usages du groupe auquel appartient le personnage.

Les motivations d'un Orc aventurier peuvent être très différentes. Certains recherchent la puissance et souhaitent prendre le commandement d'une bande, tandis que d'autres désirent obtenir un trésor, retrouver un compagnon disparu ou se venger d'un ancien supérieur. Un personnage peut chercher à survivre après la destruction de sa forteresse, transporter des informations dont plusieurs chefs souhaitent s'emparer ou rechercher une demeure éloignée des conflits. D'autres motivations sont plus exceptionnelles, particulièrement lorsqu'un Orc a rencontré un étranger qui lui a épargné la vie ou lui a apporté une aide qu'il ne s'attendait pas à recevoir. Cette expérience peut éveiller sa méfiance avant de le conduire progressivement à reconnaître la possibilité de relations différentes de celles qu'il connaissait. Il peut conserver longtemps ses anciennes habitudes, interpréter une négociation comme un affrontement et considérer la clémence comme un signe de faiblesse, tout en découvrant peu à peu que la fidélité peut reposer sur autre chose que la peur.

La place du personnage au sein d'un groupe d'aventuriers exige une attention particulière. Un Orc reconnu comme tel dans une cité humaine ou près d'une demeure elfique risque de provoquer une réaction hostile, particulièrement lorsque les habitants ont personnellement subi les violences de son peuple. Sa présence peut compromettre une mission et mettre en danger ses compagnons, même lorsque ceux-ci ont appris à lui faire confiance. Il doit donc choisir les circonstances dans lesquelles il peut se montrer, celles qui exigent de se dissimuler et celles où une confrontation paraît inévitable. Les relations établies avec les autres personnages peuvent évoluer progressivement, notamment lorsqu'une entreprise commune leur impose de dépendre les uns des autres. Un Orc peut apprendre à respecter une promesse parce que ses compagnons lui ont confié une responsabilité, tandis qu'un autre demeure attaché à ses intérêts personnels et considère chaque alliance comme un moyen de survivre dans un environnement dangereux.

Les compétences du personnage peuvent cependant rendre sa présence précieuse. Un Guerrier connaît les armes et les formations employées par sa bande, tandis qu'un Roublard peut posséder une expérience des passages dangereux, des embuscades et des déplacements furtifs. Un Voleur peut avoir appris à dissimuler des objets, franchir les obstacles et exploiter les faiblesses d'une surveillance, alors qu'un personnage formé aux métiers artisanaux dispose de connaissances techniques utiles à l'entretien des équipements. D'autres Professions peuvent être envisagées selon les compatibilités définies dans MERP-UI, particulièrement lorsque l'origine du personnage et les enseignements reçus permettent de justifier sa formation. Les disciplines magiques demeurent soumises à des conditions particulières, notamment lorsqu'elles sont liées aux puissances de l'Ombre et aux conséquences de la Corruption. Le choix d'une Profession doit ainsi prolonger une histoire personnelle cohérente, sans attribuer automatiquement au personnage les connaissances et les pouvoirs des serviteurs les plus puissants de Morgoth ou de Sauron.

L'époque de la campagne influence profondément son origine et ses possibilités. Au Premier Âge, un Orc appartient le plus souvent aux populations soumises à Morgoth et peut avoir grandi dans une forteresse ou une communauté chargée de soutenir les campagnes militaires du Seigneur des Ténèbres. Au Deuxième Âge, il peut vivre parmi les groupes dispersés après la Guerre de la Colère ou servir les ambitions croissantes de Sauron. Au Troisième Âge, son histoire peut être liée aux Monts Brumeux, à Gundabad, à la Moria, au Mordor ou aux autres établissements placés sous l'influence de l'Ombre, en tenant compte de l'apparition tardive des grandes lignées guerrières. Au Quatrième Âge, il peut appartenir aux survivants dispersés après la chute de Sauron, contraints de rechercher de nouvelles ressources et de nouvelles formes d'autorité. Ces circonstances donnent une signification particulière à son départ, particulièrement lorsqu'il doit apprendre à vivre dans un monde dont les puissances et les frontières ont profondément changé.

La Race Orcs — Yrch est disponible dans MERP-UI durant les quatre Âges de la Terre du Milieu, avec le statut de Race restreinte. Elle représente les qualités fondamentales des Orcs communs : leur constitution robuste, leur endurance, leurs sens adaptés à l'obscurité, leur sensibilité à la lumière solaire et les autres caractéristiques définies par le module. Le choix d'une Culture précise ensuite la communauté d'origine, les langues, les habitudes, les connaissances et les compétences acquises au cours de l'éducation. Les différences entre les bandes des montagnes, les garnisons du Mordor et les grandes lignées guerrières doivent demeurer conformes aux distinctions et aux compatibilités prévues dans MERP-UI. Les Demi-Orcs, issus d'ascendances mêlées avec les Hommes, constituent une Race restreinte distincte, tandis que les Uruk-hai doivent être replacés dans le contexte historique propre à leur apparition et à leurs caractéristiques.

Avant de valider la création d'un personnage orc, le joueur et le Meneur devraient déterminer la communauté dans laquelle il a grandi, l'autorité à laquelle il était soumis, sa place dans la hiérarchie et les connaissances qu'il a acquises. Ils devraient également préciser les événements qui l'ont conduit à quitter les siens, les personnes dont il demeure proche et les risques auxquels il s'expose s'il revient dans son ancienne demeure. Les conditions de sa participation à une aventure aux côtés d'autres personnages exigent une attention particulière, car son appartenance à un peuple historiquement ennemi des Peuples Libres possède des conséquences qui ne disparaissent pas au moment de la création. Le personnage doit enfin posséder des aspirations qui lui appartiennent, qu'il recherche le pouvoir, la sécurité, la richesse, la vengeance, la liberté ou la possibilité de construire une existence différente de celle qu'il a connue.

Un Orc hérite d'une histoire de domination, de violence et de servitude. Sa naissance le place généralement dans une société où la force détermine les relations et où la confiance demeure difficile à accorder. Les connaissances acquises, les personnes auxquelles il s'attache et les ambitions qu'il poursuit peuvent cependant donner à son existence des directions très différentes. Qu'il cherche à s'élever au-dessus de ses anciens compagnons, à préserver sa liberté ou à remettre en question les usages dont il a hérité, les décisions qu'il prendra, les fidélités qu'il conservera et les actes dont il acceptera la responsabilité détermineront la place qu'il occupera parmi les Yrch et dans l'histoire de la Terre du Milieu.

Orcs — The Yrch

In a gallery of the Misty Mountains, an Orcish smith examines a blade cracked near the hilt. Two warriors stand outside his workshop, arguing over ownership of the weapon. He interrupts them with a growl and points at the fracture with his tongs: the repair will require more metal than they have brought him. He indicates a heap of broken pieces recovered after a skirmish and orders them to find something he can use to complete the work. The warriors protest, but the captain of their band has demanded that every weapon be ready before the next expedition. They eventually obey, while the smith turns the blade in the furnace and instructs his apprentice to work the bellows. The workshop stands beside a gallery through which porters carry supplies to the storerooms. Deliveries have been scarce for several days, and fuel is beginning to run low. The smith knows that his captain will hold him personally responsible for any delay, even if the necessary materials have not been provided. He therefore examines the weapons abandoned against the wall and selects those from which he can salvage the best parts. His apprentice asks whether they too will accompany the next company. He tells him to prepare the tools first, for the wounded will certainly bring back more weapons in need of repair.

Farther into the mountains, a small company makes its way through a steep passage. Its captain is searching for an ancient path leading towards the inhabited valleys, where several caravans have been reported since the return of warmer weather. A scout walks ahead, followed by a porter carrying provisions and two archers watching the heights. They have been marching for several hours and are beginning to run short of water. When the scout discovers a spring, the captain orders him to examine the surrounding ground before allowing the company to halt. His soldiers obey reluctantly. One suggests returning to the caverns, but his neighbour reminds him what awaits soldiers who return without plunder. The captain knows the Orcs under his command: two remain loyal because he has provided them with better weapons, a third hopes to take his place, and the others chiefly wish to survive until the spoils are divided. Above the ridges, the first light of day begins to appear. They must quickly reach a sheltered passage, for several of his companions have difficulty enduring sunlight. The captain orders them to march again, despite their protests, and takes care to remain behind those whom he trusts least.

These Orcs belong to the Yrch, a people whose history remains closely bound to that of Morgoth and Sauron. Their bands inhabit caverns, fortresses, and territories abandoned by other peoples, while their armies have taken part in the greatest wars of Middle-earth. They possess a robust constitution, remarkable endurance, and senses adapted to darkness, but their communities display considerable differences in stature, strength, and organisation. Most live under the authority of chiefs who impose their power through violence, while others belong to groups far removed from the great realms of the Shadow, subsisting upon the resources of their territories and the expeditions they undertake. Their history is that of a people subjected for Ages to domination, warfare, and rivalry, whose individuals have learned to survive in societies where strength often determines each person's place. Yet behind the armies and bands feared by the Free Peoples are also craftsmen, labourers, scouts, and individuals whose personal concerns are seldom mentioned in the great chronicles.

The Uncertain Origins of the Orcs

The origin of the Yrch remains one of the most difficult questions in the history of Middle-earth. All accounts assign a fundamental role to Morgoth, the first Dark Lord, who sought to gather servants capable of fighting the Children of Ilúvatar, populating his fortresses, and extending his authority over the lands he coveted. Morgoth possessed the power to deform living beings, corrupt their nature, and subjugate their wills, but the creation of a truly independent existence remained the prerogative of Eru Ilúvatar. This limitation gives the origin of the Orcs a significance extending beyond their own history, since it concerns the nature of their spirits and their responsibility for their actions. The surviving accounts do not, however, establish with certainty the means by which Morgoth succeeded in forming the earliest Orcish populations.

According to a tradition recounted in The Silmarillion, Elves captured shortly after their awakening were taken into the depths of Utumno, where Morgoth subjected them to prolonged torture and transformations intended to destroy their original nature. Their descendants are said to have become the ancestors of the Orcs, raised in hatred of the Eldar and employed in the enterprises of the Dark Lord. Tolkien nevertheless considered other possibilities in his later writings, including an origin among Men or populations derived from several sources, some of which might have been subjected to the influence of spiritual servants of Morgoth. These reflections never resulted in a definitively established solution. The chronology of the awakening of the peoples, the nature of corrupted beings, and the question of their independent wills remained difficulties that the author continued to examine.

This uncertainty deserves to be preserved in MERP-UI. An Orc may have received from his elders an account of a particular origin without possessing any means of verifying its truth. Some pass down stories concerning ancestors fashioned in the depths of Morgoth's fortresses, while others know confused traditions referring to transformed captives or populations torn from their homelands. Most define themselves chiefly through membership of a band, fortress, or local lineage whose rivalries and former chiefs they remember. Their origins nevertheless retain one essential consequence: Orcish populations were raised for centuries in servitude and violence. Morgoth, and later Sauron, sought to convince them that the other peoples were their natural enemies and that their security depended entirely upon the power of their masters. This inheritance explains much of their traditions without entirely resolving the question of individual will, which remains one of the most complex aspects of portraying them.

From Morgoth's Fortresses to the Armies of Sauron

The first Orcs appeared in Morgoth's fortresses before the great wars of Beleriand. Utumno, his ancient underground stronghold, housed the servants and creatures he prepared for his enterprises, while Angband subsequently became the principal centre of his power in the northern regions. Orcs were employed in maintaining fortifications, extracting resources, and manufacturing the equipment intended for the armies. They learned to fight under captains more powerful than themselves, construct military works, and travel through the territories Morgoth sought to conquer. Their numbers constituted an essential resource, particularly when their masters launched offensives against fortresses whose defenders possessed superior weapons and knowledge.

During the First Age, Orcish armies took part in the wars against the Sindar and subsequently against the Noldor who had returned from Aman. They participated in Morgoth's great offensives, ravaged settlements, and pursued populations forced to abandon their homes. Their troops fought under Orcish captains, but also under Balrogs, Dragons, and other servants of the Dark Lord. Losses were considerable, for the masters of Angband often treated their soldiers as expendable resources, imposing exhausting marches and punishing those who refused their orders. The War of Wrath finally brought about the collapse of this power and the dispersal of the survivors, some of whom found refuge in mountains, caverns, and remote regions. Their history thereafter continued in different forms, between relatively independent bands and populations gradually gathered under the authority of Sauron, Morgoth's former servant.

Throughout the following Ages, the Yrch took part in Sauron's enterprises while preserving communities whose interests did not always coincide with those of the Dark Lord. Some bands exploited the resources of their territories, organised their own expeditions, and sought to escape the demands of greater powers. Others became the garrisons of fortresses, the workers of arsenals, and the soldiers of Mordor's armies. These differences explain the diversity of experiences available to an Orcish character: an individual raised in a garrison subjected to strict military discipline does not necessarily know the same customs as an inhabitant of the Misty Mountains, whose chief must preserve his authority through dealings with several rival bands. All nevertheless inherit a history dominated by warfare and the relationships of power imposed over generations.

A Robust Constitution Shaped by Darkness

Orcs possess a humanoid appearance, but their proportions vary considerably between populations. Ordinary individuals are generally shorter than Men, with stocky bodies, powerful shoulders, relatively long arms, and legs that are sometimes short or bowed. Their musculature favours sustained exertion, carrying burdens, and wielding weapons suited to their stature. Their faces often feature pronounced jaws, prominent brow ridges, and irregular teeth, while their skin colour varies according to lineage, from greyish and brownish tones to darker or yellowish shades. Their hair is generally dark, sometimes sparse, and scars are common among individuals who have spent many years fighting or working under dangerous conditions. These characteristics are not uniform, however: the mountain populations, those of Mordor, and the great warrior lineages developed during the Third Age display noticeable differences.

The endurance of the Yrch allows them to march for many hours, carry heavy burdens, and continue exerting themselves despite fatigue. This resilience explains their employment in underground works and military campaigns, but also leads their masters to impose excessive demands upon them. Their bodies remain vulnerable to wounds, disease, and deprivation, particularly when their living conditions prevent individuals from receiving adequate care. Their exact longevity is not established by Tolkien. MERP developments envisage a potential lifespan exceeding that of ordinary Men, but warfare, internal violence, and the dangers of their work make it particularly rare for an Orc to survive to an advanced age. Elders may nevertheless preserve valuable knowledge of galleries, routes, and rivalries between bands, even when their authority remains threatened by the ambitions of younger individuals.

Their senses are particularly adapted to darkness. Orcs can distinguish shapes and movements in dimly lit caverns, while their familiarity with underground passages allows them to recognise details that would escape foreign travellers. Their sense of smell may also help them identify a trail or recognise an unusual presence, particularly when a character possesses genuine tracking experience. Sunlight, by contrast, presents a considerable difficulty for many common Orcs. Its brightness is painful to them and may substantially reduce their effectiveness, leading them to favour night marches, overcast days, and sheltered passages. This sensitivity does not cause their destruction in daylight, and certain populations may be compelled to fight despite the discomfort. The great warrior lineages appearing later sometimes display greater tolerance, but their particular qualities must remain distinct from those of the common Race.

Caverns, Lairs, and Fortresses

Orcs inhabit widely differing dwellings, from natural caverns to great fortresses built or conquered in the service of their masters. In the mountains, settlements often develop around ancient galleries, which the inhabitants enlarge to accommodate storerooms, workshops, and defensive passages. Entrances are carefully chosen, particularly when a steep slope or narrow opening makes it possible to watch for approaching strangers. Large communities possess common halls, storage areas, metalworking workshops, and guard posts, while captains generally occupy the best-protected chambers. Labourers and soldiers of lower rank often live under considerably harsher conditions, among crowded passages, rudimentary sleeping places, and installations whose maintenance depends upon the available resources. Smoke from hearths, refuse, and accumulated goods make certain galleries particularly unhealthy when ventilation is inadequate.

The quality of these installations varies according to the organisation of the communities. A fortress of Sauron possesses stores, military posts, and thoroughfares suited to the needs of a large army, while an independent lair in the Misty Mountains depends more directly upon the means available to its chief. Work may be carried out by craftsmen, soldiers assigned to labour duties, or prisoners forced to undertake the most dangerous tasks. Certain bands also occupy ruins and settlements abandoned by other peoples, salvaging their materials and altering their defences. Knowledge of the passages then represents a valuable advantage, for an inhabitant may know the locations of secondary entrances, concealed stores, and galleries that have become dangerous. For a character, such a dwelling is the place of his childhood, earliest apprenticeships, and personal relationships, but also the home of the chiefs he fears, the rivals whose anger he seeks to avoid, and the individuals to whom he remains attached.

A Society Ruled by Strength

Orcish communities are generally organised into brutal hierarchies, in which authority rests upon strength, fear, and the ability to maintain supporters. A chief rules his band because he possesses the means to compel obedience, whether through his military reputation, control of the stores, or support from particularly formidable warriors. He determines the expeditions, distributes plunder, and entrusts captains with watching passages or commanding patrols. His lieutenants often receive better weapons, larger portions of food, and privileged access to goods recovered during raids. Less powerful individuals occupy far more precarious positions, particularly when they enjoy no personal protection and must carry out the tasks imposed by their superiors.

This organisation sustains almost constant rivalry. Chiefs watch the ambitions of their lieutenants, warriors seek to improve their position, and workers must sometimes conceal their possessions to avoid being robbed. Physical strength remains important, but does not always suffice to preserve power. A captain incapable of finding provisions or leading his band through dangerous territory may quickly lose his authority, while a less imposing individual sometimes becomes indispensable through technical knowledge, mastery of passages, or relationships with other groups. Alliances between chiefs generally rest upon immediate advantage, particularly when a raid promises riches or a common enemy threatens several settlements. Under a powerful master, discipline may be reinforced by fear of punishment, without rivalries between garrisons disappearing altogether.

An Orc raised within this society learns very early to recognise dangerous individuals and understand the relationships of power governing daily life. He knows that an apparently ordinary order may conceal a rivalry between officers, that a favour received from one chief may arouse another's jealousy, and that possessing a valuable object sometimes demands as much caution as obtaining it. Some develop a remarkable ability to observe behaviour and anticipate conflict, while others seek authority themselves in order to escape dependence upon others. These habits profoundly influence characters who leave their communities, particularly when they discover societies in which responsibilities may rest upon principles other than coercion and threats.

Families and Generations

Tolkien's accounts chiefly present Orcs as soldiers and very rarely describe their family lives. Their reproduction is nevertheless established, since Orcs multiply in the manner of other living peoples, and the existence of female Orcs was confirmed by Tolkien without their social roles being developed in his stories. MERP supplements have proposed more precise forms of organisation, including communities in which reproduction and the upbringing of the young remain closely subject to the authority of chiefs. These descriptions may provide a foundation for a campaign, but do not constitute universal institutions directly established by Tolkien. Their diversity allows different family experiences to be envisaged according to the size of a community, its degree of militarisation, and the relationships of power prevailing within it.

In a great fortress, education may chiefly answer the needs of the masters. The young learn to recognise orders, carry burdens, and perform the work required to maintain the installations, before being gradually directed towards military or craft activities according to their dispositions and the decisions of their superiors. In a small mountain community, instruction may be more direct: a child accompanies adults gathering fuel, inspecting traps, or repairing passages, gradually learning to recognise the dangers and resources of his surroundings. These apprenticeships remain exposed to the ordinary violence of Orcish society, particularly when food and protection depend closely upon the position occupied by families. An adult may seek to protect a child from a captain's demands, while a young Orc learns to conceal his mistakes to avoid punishments whose consequences he knows well.

Such conditions do not exclude personal attachments. An Orc may preserve the memory of a parent, protect a weaker companion, or remain attached to someone who taught him his trade. These relationships are nevertheless vulnerable to pressure exerted by chiefs, particularly when protecting a loved one requires relinquishing a reward or disobeying an order. A character may thus have grown up beside someone towards whom he feels profound gratitude, while also having learned to regard trust as a risk. His family history constitutes an important part of his portrayal, for it helps determine the loyalties he preserves, the people he fears, and the events that might lead him to leave his community.

Trades, Resources, and Daily Life

Orcs possess considerable technical skills, particularly in constructing fortresses, working metal, and manufacturing military equipment. Their forges produce blades, spearheads, pieces of armour, and objects needed to maintain defensive works. Craftsmen readily salvage materials captured from enemies, repair damaged weapons, and manufacture parts intended to withstand the repeated stresses of combat. Their creations may possess a crude or threatening appearance, but their effectiveness demands genuine mastery of the techniques employed. Certain workshops produce sturdy mechanisms, chains, and siege components capable of withstanding considerable strain, while military engineers know how to adapt their constructions to the requirements of a campaign. Such skill is often accompanied by a pursuit of immediate efficiency, particularly when captains impose short deadlines and possess limited resources.

Leatherworking, woodworking, and stoneworking complement these activities. Craftsmen make protective equipment, straps, containers, and the gear required for travel, while cavern labourers maintain galleries, transport materials, and clear obstructed passages. Sustaining the communities also requires regular organisation. Provisions may come from hunting, livestock breeding, gathering, certain underground crops, or supplies furnished by military masters. MERP developments mention, in particular, mushrooms cultivated in caverns and herds maintained in mountainous regions. Plunder constitutes another important source of resources, especially for bands established near territories inhabited by other peoples. Raids make it possible to obtain food, clothing, weapons, and materials, some of which are then used to reward warriors and maintain their loyalty.

The distribution of resources remains closely connected with the hierarchy. Captains generally secure the best portions and most precious objects, while soldiers and workers of lower rank receive whatever remains available. An unsuccessful expedition may provoke deprivation, quarrels, and accusations intended to identify those responsible for failure. Under such circumstances, certain individuals become indispensable through their abilities. A smith capable of keeping weapons serviceable, a guide familiar with mountain paths, or a keeper of stores skilled at preventing waste may acquire influence greater than his physical strength would normally have allowed. His position nevertheless remains fragile, for recognition of his usefulness often depends upon the needs and temper of the chiefs. A character may thus possess a respected trade and still seek to leave his community when his work no longer protects him against the ambitions of his superiors.

The Languages of the Bands and the Black Speech

Orcs possess no single language that has remained unchanged since the earliest days of their history. Their communities have developed numerous forms of speech, often composed of elements borrowed from other languages and transformed over generations. Idioms differ according to territories, bands, and periods, particularly when populations scatter after defeat or gather under new chiefs. Two groups originating from distant mountains may therefore have great difficulty understanding one another, their expressions and vocabulary having evolved in different directions. Terms used to describe weapons, ranks, provisions, and the dangers of the territory may vary considerably, while certain expressions preserve the memory of departed chiefs or events particular to a community.

Sauron sought to limit this diversity by devising the Black Speech, intended to serve as a common language among his subjects. Its use was particularly associated with Mordor and communities placed under the Dark Lord's direct domination, but it never entirely replaced local idioms. Soldiers of different origins sometimes employ Westron, in corrupted forms, to transmit orders or converse among themselves. The vocabulary of the hierarchy also preserves important terms: uruk means Orc in the Black Speech and is used, according to circumstances, to distinguish certain great warrior lineages, while snaga, meaning slave, may be employed contemptuously towards individuals considered inferior. The Elves call Orcs Yrch, whose singular form is Orch, while the term Goblins frequently appears in accounts concerning underground populations. In Tolkien's writings, these last two designations do not correspond to fundamentally distinct Races.

Mastery of languages depends upon personal experience. A guard who has always lived within the same fortress may know only his community's speech and a few military expressions, while a scout regularly sent into foreign territories learns to recognise several idioms. An experienced captain may identify an interlocutor's probable origins from his accent, and a trader accustomed to dealings between bands may employ several languages in negotiation. Such knowledge becomes particularly important for an Orcish adventurer, especially when he wishes to travel, transmit information, or escape the surveillance of former masters capable of recognising his connection with a particular garrison.

Beliefs and the Dominion of the Shadow

The spiritual life of Orcs remains profoundly marked by their long servitude. Morgoth imposed his power upon their ancestors, and Sauron later perpetuated this domination by presenting his authority as the only possible protection against the enemies surrounding their communities. In certain fortresses, the symbols of the Dark Lord, the orders transmitted in his name, and the punishments inflicted upon the disobedient maintain constant fear. MERP supplements also develop practices in which certain Orcs honour power, darkness, or domination, sometimes under the guidance of individuals fulfilling ritual functions. These traditions do not, however, constitute a single universal religion described by Tolkien. Beliefs may differ according to bands, periods, and relationships maintained with the powers of the Shadow.

The feelings of Orcs towards their masters remain contradictory. Some willingly seek the support of Sauron or his servants to obtain rewards and increase their authority, while others obey through fear of punishment and would prefer to live far from the great armies. Such hostility towards their own chiefs does not necessarily mean that they wish to renounce the violence committed against other peoples. An individual may hate servitude while still regarding plunder and domination as ordinary means of securing his livelihood. The disappearance of a Dark Lord therefore leaves deeply rooted habits intact, particularly when several generations have known only organisations founded upon strength. Characters wishing to turn away from this inheritance must confront genuine difficulties, without their personal will being wholly determined by the traditions they received.

Magic constitutes a particularly dangerous field for ordinary Orcs. Certain servants of the Shadow possess occult knowledge, employ objects associated with the powers of Morgoth and Sauron, or practise rituals passed down within particular communities. Individuals receiving such instruction may acquire considerable influence, but their dependence upon their masters often becomes more profound. In MERP-UI, the magical possibilities of an Orcish character remain subject to authorised Professions, the teachings received, and RMU rules. Membership of this Race grants no spontaneous mastery of Sorcery, Essence, Mentalism, or Channeling, while traditions connected with the Shadow and Corruption retain the consequences defined by the module.

The Mountain Orcs

Orcish populations established in the Misty Mountains and Grey Mountains number among the best known in the northern regions. Their communities inhabit caverns, ancient mines, and fortresses situated near mountain passes, whose positions they sometimes exploit to watch travellers and organise ambushes. Mount Gundabad holds a particularly important place in their history, while the galleries of Moria became one of their principal settlements after the abandonment of Khazad-dûm. These communities may maintain commercial or military relationships, but their chiefs often pursue competing interests. Control of a road, mineral vein, or hunting territory may provoke conflict, particularly when one band seeks to seize the resources of a neighbouring group. Expeditions against caravans, human settlements, and Dwarven communities provide a regular source of plunder, but also require preparation intended to avoid military forces too powerful to confront.

Certain Orcs maintain relationships with Wolves and Wargs, which they may employ for hunting, travel, or combat. Handling these creatures requires particular experience and remains dangerous, even for individuals accustomed to their presence. The great campaigns against the Khazâd also demonstrate the military capabilities of the mountain populations. The death of Thrór, slain in Moria by Azog, provoked the War of the Dwarves and Orcs, which culminated in the Battle of Azanulbizar, where Azog was killed by Dáin Ironfoot. Later, Bolg, son of Azog, gathered a considerable force to intervene at the foot of Erebor during the events leading to the Battle of Five Armies. These enterprises demonstrate that mountain bands could unite under a common command and organise major expeditions, even when their chiefs were not acting directly under Sauron's orders.

The Orcs of Mordor and the Great Warrior Lineages

The Orcs of Mordor live in surroundings profoundly marked by Sauron's authority. The fortresses of the Ephel Dúath, the Ered Lithui, and the outposts guarding the approaches to the land contain garrisons charged with defending the borders, controlling passages, and participating in military operations. Captains receive their orders from superiors whose authority is connected with Barad-dûr, while soldiers are subjected to strict demands concerning movement, discipline, and the execution of missions. Rivalries nevertheless remain numerous, particularly when several garrisons seek the favour of their masters or the possession of plunder. The events involving Shagrat and Gorbag during the War of the Ring demonstrate how dangerous these tensions could become, even between troops belonging to the same power.

Mordor also possesses Orcs specialising in reconnaissance and tracking, whose qualities differ from those of the most imposing fighters. Some are smaller than the warriors of the garrisons, but their knowledge of the terrain, sense of smell, and ability to recognise a trail make them particularly useful. During the Third Age, great warrior lineages also appear, known as Uruks or Uruk-hai according to usage and circumstance. The first great black Uruks of Mordor are recorded in T.A. 2475, during the invasion of Ithilien and the capture of Osgiliath. Taller and more powerful than many common Orcs, they are particularly suited to the demands of warfare against well-equipped adversaries. Later, Saruman gathers his own troops of Uruk-hai at Isengard, capable of enduring long marches and better tolerating exposure to sunlight.

These populations must be distinguished from common Orcs, particularly when their physical characteristics and military training differ from those of the older bands. The crossing of Orcs and Men undertaken by Saruman is likewise a separate matter and gives rise to individuals of mixed ancestry represented separately among the Half-orcs, a Restricted Race of MERP-UI. Chronology remains essential: the great warrior lineages appearing towards the end of the Third Age cannot indiscriminately be attributed to the armies of earlier periods. Their use must therefore respect the historical distinctions and compatibilities established by the module, without altering the fundamental characteristics of the common Orc Race.

The Yrch Through the Ages

During the First Age, Orcs constitute a considerable part of Morgoth's military forces. Their existence remains closely connected with the Dark Lord's fortresses and the campaigns conducted against the Elven and human kingdoms of Beleriand. Individuals may serve as soldiers, craftsmen, guards, or labourers under captains whose power generally exceeds that of local chiefs. The War of Wrath subsequently brings about the destruction of their great armies and the dispersal of survivors. During the Second Age, some communities remain far removed from the principal powers, while Sauron begins gathering new forces and establishing Mordor as the centre of his authority. Orcs participate in the wars against the Elves and Númenóreans, while preserving mountain populations whose interests sometimes remain independent.

During the Third Age, Orcs inhabit numerous regions, notably the Misty Mountains, the Grey Mountains, Gundabad, Moria, Angmar, Dol Guldur, and Mordor. Some bands live by plunder and the resources of their territories, while others are incorporated into Sauron's armies or serve the ambitions of his allies. Wars against the Khazâd, attacks upon human settlements, and the great campaigns at the end of this Age bring about considerable movements of population. The War of the Ring finally marks the height and subsequent collapse of Orcish military power in Sauron's service, whose disappearance leads to the disorganisation of numerous garrisons.

During the Fourth Age, survivors must continue their existence in a profoundly transformed world. Many have perished, others have fled into the mountains and remote regions, while the ancient fortresses of the Shadow lose their power. The remaining bands must secure new resources, establish new authorities, and confront the growing strength of the kingdoms of Men. Tolkien's accounts do not precisely describe their subsequent fate, leaving the Gamemaster free to explore the consequences of this disappearance for Orcish communities. A character may belong to the last soldiers of an abandoned garrison, the inhabitants of a mountain settlement that remained relatively independent, or a company seeking to rebuild its existence after losing its former master. Such possibilities belong to developments particular to the campaign, especially when they lead to the consideration of new relationships with other peoples.

Among the Other Peoples of Middle-earth

The relationships of Orcs with other peoples are dominated by centuries of warfare and violence. The Elves number among their oldest enemies, and stories passed down within the bands often portray them as cruel adversaries determined to destroy the Yrch. This representation was fostered by the masters of the Shadow, who sought to convince their servants that no mercy could be expected from the Eldar. The Khazâd constitute other formidable adversaries, particularly in mountainous regions where territorial conflicts, attacks upon mines, and wars fought around Moria have nourished profound hostility. Orcs know the strength of Dwarven warriors and the quality of their weapons, while the descendants of Durin preserve the memory of the dead and the destruction caused by Orcish bands.

Relationships with Men are more varied, but generally remain hostile. Border populations suffer plundering, abductions, and attacks, while certain human communities themselves serve the powers of the Shadow and fight alongside Orcs. These alliances nevertheless erase neither the rivalries nor the contempt that often exist between warriors of different origins. The Dúnedain remain among the most constant adversaries of the Yrch, particularly when they protect lands threatened by their expeditions. Hobbits chiefly know Orcs through tales or dangers encountered during journeys, their small stature making them vulnerable when captured, but their stealth sometimes allowing them to escape more numerous pursuers. Relationships between Orcish bands may be just as contentious as those they maintain with other peoples, especially when territorial disputes or rivalries between chiefs provoke deadly confrontations.

An Orcish adventurer must therefore contend with almost universal hostility. His appearance may immediately provoke fear, even when he has committed no offence against those he encounters. He may be pursued by the servants of the Shadow after desertion, then rejected by inhabitants of the free lands where he seeks refuge. Companions who accept his presence must also take account of the reactions it will provoke, particularly when a mission requires passing through the gates of a city or gaining the trust of a community previously attacked by Orcs. New relationships must therefore be built through deeds, commitments honoured, and experiences shared, without erasing the historical consequences of the character's belonging to his people.

Fear, Cruelty, and the Freedom to Choose

Tolkien generally presents Orcs as cruel, quarrelsome beings, quick to exploit the weakness of others. These behaviours are deeply rooted in their history, for generations have lived within societies where domination, punishment, and violence constitute the principal means of enforcing authority. Fear plays an essential role in these relationships. A soldier obeys a captain he hates because he knows the consequences of refusal, a craftsman accepts excessive demands to preserve his workshop, and a scout conceals a mistake when he knows that his superior would seek to make an example of him. This fear sustains mistrust between individuals, particularly when denouncing a companion offers the possibility of a reward or a chief encourages rivalries to prevent conspiracies against his authority.

Some Orcs willingly participate in this violence and seek to increase their power, while others conform because they have never known another form of organisation or fear becoming victims of their companions themselves. The accounts nevertheless show that they may experience personal desires distinct from the ambitions of their masters. Some wish to retain a share of the plunder, leave a garrison, or live in a region far removed from the great wars. This desire to free themselves from orders does not necessarily accompany a wish to abandon the brutal habits acquired throughout their existence. An Orc deserting Sauron's armies may simply seek his own safety, wish to command a band, or seize a territory whose resources he intends to control.

The question of their individual responsibility remains delicate within Tolkien's world, for the author himself continued to reflect upon the moral nature of Orcs and the consequences of their origins. Two essential aspects should therefore be preserved: their existence was profoundly shaped by the dominion of the Shadow, but their actions and decisions must not be presented as mere movements entirely devoid of will. A character may remain cruel, pursue personal ambitions, or seek to reproduce the relationships of power he has always known. Within a campaign, he may also encounter circumstances leading him to question certain habits. Such a development demands genuine experiences, decisions, and consequences, particularly when the character must learn to understand relationships founded upon trust rather than fear.

Playing an Orc

Playing an Orc in Middle-earth means portraying a character whose existence is profoundly marked by a hostile society, dangerous relationships of power, and a heritage associated with the forces of the Shadow. His constitution grants him remarkable physical qualities, but his upbringing determines the knowledge he actually possesses and the behaviours he has learned. A young Orc may have grown up in the galleries of the Misty Mountains, where he knows his community's passages, the paths followed by patrols, and the places where resources needed to sustain his band may be found. He has learned to obey chiefs, recognise their rivalries, and keep his possessions beyond the reach of more powerful individuals. His departure may result from a quarrel, the disappearance of the captain who protected him, or an expedition from which he was the sole survivor. He may also have received a reconnaissance mission in a distant region and discovered, after an unforeseen event, that returning would present greater dangers than continuing his journey.

Another character may belong to the garrisons of Mordor, where he has received military training and learned the signals employed in fortresses. His superiors expect strict obedience, particularly when he must guard a passage, accompany a convoy, or take part in an operation against Sauron's enemies. Desertion then becomes a particularly perilous undertaking, since he must escape the surveillance of his former companions and avoid routes frequented by his master's troops. He may know the military practices of the armies of the Shadow and possess valuable information concerning their fortifications, but revealing it also risks marking him as a traitor in the eyes of other Orcs. His existence then depends upon his ability to find a region where he can survive, particularly when his appearance closes most refuges among the Free Peoples to him.

An Orcish craftsman possesses different experience. He has spent many years in a forge, leatherworking shop, or establishment responsible for maintaining military machinery. He knows metals, mechanisms, and objects salvaged during raids, while his work gives him a usefulness recognised by the chiefs of his community. Such skill may protect him from certain forms of violence, but also exposes him to the demands of superiors who expect immediate results and possess the power to deprive him of his tools. His departure may be provoked by a conflict with a captain, the search for materials difficult to obtain, or the desire to preserve an object his superior intends to appropriate. He may also wish to offer his services to another band, particularly when he believes his knowledge will enable him to obtain a more favourable position.

A scout may possess extensive knowledge of a territory, particularly when he has spent several years searching for passages, watching caravans, and observing the movements of neighbouring populations. He knows how to recognise signs left by a company, find a passable route during the night, and choose a position suitable for an ambush. These skills may enable him to survive far from his community, but also expose him to the dangers of the regions he crosses. A female Orc from an underground settlement may have learned to manage stores, maintain equipment, or organise certain activities necessary for communal life. According to the developments adopted by the Gamemaster, her education may include hunting, crafts, or techniques for defending her community. The scarcity of information concerning female Orcs in Tolkien's writings leaves room for interpretation, whose details must remain consistent with the customs of the group to which the character belongs.

The motivations of an Orcish adventurer may differ greatly. Some seek power and wish to command a band, while others desire treasure, hope to find a missing companion, or seek revenge upon a former superior. A character may struggle to survive after the destruction of his fortress, carry information that several chiefs wish to seize, or seek a dwelling far removed from conflict. Other motivations are more exceptional, particularly when an Orc has encountered a stranger who spared his life or offered assistance he never expected to receive. This experience may initially arouse his suspicion before gradually leading him to recognise the possibility of relationships different from those he previously knew. He may long preserve his old habits, interpret negotiation as a confrontation, and regard mercy as a sign of weakness, while slowly discovering that loyalty can rest upon something other than fear.

The character's place within a company of adventurers requires particular attention. An Orc recognised as such in a human city or near an Elven dwelling risks provoking a hostile reaction, especially when the inhabitants have personally suffered violence at the hands of his people. His presence may compromise a mission and endanger his companions, even when they have learned to trust him. He must therefore choose the circumstances in which he can reveal himself, those requiring concealment, and those in which confrontation seems unavoidable. Relationships established with the other characters may gradually develop, particularly when a shared undertaking requires them to depend upon one another. An Orc may learn to honour a promise because his companions have entrusted him with a responsibility, while another remains attached to his personal interests and regards every alliance as a means of surviving in a dangerous environment.

The character's skills may nevertheless make his presence valuable. A Fighter knows the weapons and formations employed by his band, while a Rogue may possess experience of dangerous passages, ambushes, and stealthy movement. A Thief may have learned to conceal objects, negotiate obstacles, and exploit weaknesses in surveillance, while a character trained in crafts possesses technical knowledge useful for maintaining equipment. Other Professions may be considered according to the compatibilities established in MERP-UI, particularly when the character's origins and the instruction he received justify his training. Magical disciplines remain subject to particular conditions, especially when connected with the powers of the Shadow and the consequences of Corruption. The choice of a Profession must therefore continue a coherent personal history, without automatically attributing to the character the knowledge and powers of the most formidable servants of Morgoth or Sauron.

The period of the campaign profoundly influences his origins and possibilities. During the First Age, an Orc most often belongs to populations subjected to Morgoth and may have grown up in a fortress or community charged with supporting the Dark Lord's military campaigns. During the Second Age, he may live among groups scattered after the War of Wrath or serve Sauron's growing ambitions. During the Third Age, his history may be connected with the Misty Mountains, Gundabad, Moria, Mordor, or other settlements under the influence of the Shadow, taking account of the late appearance of the great warrior lineages. During the Fourth Age, he may belong to survivors scattered after Sauron's downfall, forced to seek new resources and new forms of authority. These circumstances give particular significance to his departure, especially when he must learn to live in a world whose powers and borders have profoundly changed.

The Orcs — Yrch Race is available in MERP-UI throughout the four Ages of Middle-earth, with the status of a Restricted Race. It represents the fundamental qualities of common Orcs: their robust constitution, endurance, senses adapted to darkness, sensitivity to sunlight, and the other characteristics defined by the module. The choice of a Culture then determines the community of origin, languages, habits, knowledge, and skills acquired during upbringing. Differences between mountain bands, the garrisons of Mordor, and the great warrior lineages must remain consistent with the distinctions and compatibilities established in MERP-UI. Half-orcs, descended from mixed ancestry with Men, constitute a separate Restricted Race, while the Uruk-hai must be placed within the historical context particular to their appearance and characteristics.

Before approving the creation of an Orcish character, the player and Gamemaster should determine the community in which he grew up, the authority to which he was subjected, his place within the hierarchy, and the knowledge he acquired. They should also establish the events that led him to leave his people, those to whom he remains close, and the risks he would face should he return to his former dwelling. The conditions of his participation in an adventure alongside other characters require particular attention, for belonging to a people historically hostile to the Free Peoples carries consequences that do not disappear at character creation. Finally, the character must possess aspirations of his own, whether he seeks power, security, wealth, revenge, freedom, or the possibility of building an existence different from the one he has known.

An Orc inherits a history of domination, violence, and servitude. His birth generally places him in a society where strength determines relationships and trust is difficult to grant. The knowledge he acquires, the people to whom he becomes attached, and the ambitions he pursues may nevertheless give his existence very different directions. Whether he seeks to rise above his former companions, preserve his freedom, or question the customs he has inherited, the decisions he makes, the loyalties he maintains, and the deeds for which he accepts responsibility will determine the place he occupies among the Yrch and in the history of Middle-earth.

talents.description: Les Orcs voient efficacement dans les souterrains et conservent une perception limitée dans l’obscurité presque totale.

talents.name: Tireless
talents.description: Ils supportent les marches forcées, la faim, le manque de sommeil et les mauvais traitements.

talents.name: Temperature Resistance
talents.description: Ils résistent bien aux chaleurs et froids naturels.

talents.name: Sunlight Sensitivity
talents.description: La lumière solaire directe réduit fortement leur efficacité et provoque douleur, fatigue et désorientation.

talents.name: Water Aversion
talents.description: Les eaux profondes et courantes provoquent une peur et une gêne marquées.

system.description:
Orcs — Les Yrch

Dans une galerie des Monts Brumeux, un forgeron orc examine une lame fendue près de la garde. Deux guerriers attendent devant son atelier, occupés à se disputer la propriété de l'arme. Il les interrompt d'un grognement et désigne la fissure du bout de ses pinces : la réparation exigera davantage de métal que ce qu'ils lui ont apporté. Il leur indique un amas de pièces brisées, récupérées après une escarmouche, et leur ordonne d'y chercher de quoi compléter son travail. Les guerriers protestent, mais le capitaine de leur bande a exigé que toutes les armes soient prêtes avant la prochaine expédition. Ils finissent par obéir, tandis que le forgeron retourne la lame dans le foyer et demande à son apprenti d'actionner les soufflets. L'atelier est installé près d'une galerie où circulent les porteurs chargés d'approvisionner les réserves. Depuis plusieurs jours, les arrivages se font rares et le combustible commence à manquer. Le forgeron sait que son capitaine lui imputera personnellement tout retard, même si les matériaux nécessaires ne lui ont pas été fournis. Il examine donc les armes abandonnées contre la paroi et choisit celles dont il pourra récupérer les meilleures pièces. Son apprenti lui demande s'ils partiront eux aussi avec la prochaine troupe. Il lui répond de préparer d'abord les outils, car les blessés rapporteront certainement d'autres armes à réparer.

Plus loin dans les montagnes, une petite compagnie progresse à travers un passage escarpé. Son capitaine recherche un ancien sentier conduisant vers les vallées habitées, où plusieurs caravanes ont été signalées depuis le retour des beaux jours. Un éclaireur marche en tête, suivi d'un porteur chargé des vivres et de deux archers qui surveillent les hauteurs. Ils avancent depuis plusieurs heures et commencent à manquer d'eau. Lorsque l'éclaireur découvre une source, le capitaine lui ordonne d'examiner les environs avant d'autoriser la halte. Les membres de sa troupe obéissent avec mauvaise grâce. L'un d'eux propose de retourner vers les cavernes, mais son voisin lui rappelle ce qui attend les soldats qui reviennent sans butin. Le capitaine connaît les hommes placés sous ses ordres : deux lui sont fidèles parce qu'il leur a procuré de meilleures armes, un troisième espère prendre sa place et les autres cherchent surtout à survivre jusqu'au partage des prises. Au-dessus des crêtes, les premières lueurs du jour apparaissent. Il leur faut rapidement rejoindre un passage couvert, car plusieurs de ses compagnons supportent difficilement la lumière du soleil. Le capitaine ordonne une nouvelle marche, malgré les protestations, et prend soin de demeurer derrière ceux auxquels il accorde le moins de confiance.

Ces Orcs appartiennent aux Yrch, un peuple dont l'histoire demeure étroitement liée à celle de Morgoth et de Sauron. Leurs bandes occupent des cavernes, des forteresses et des territoires abandonnés par d'autres peuples, tandis que leurs armées ont participé aux plus grandes guerres de la Terre du Milieu. Ils possèdent une constitution robuste, une endurance remarquable et des sens adaptés à l'obscurité, mais leurs communautés présentent des différences considérables de stature, de force et d'organisation. La plupart vivent sous l'autorité de chefs qui imposent leur pouvoir par la violence, tandis que d'autres appartiennent à des groupes éloignés des grands royaumes de l'Ombre, subsistant grâce aux ressources de leur territoire et aux expéditions qu'ils organisent. Leur histoire est celle d'un peuple soumis pendant des âges à la domination, à la guerre et à la rivalité, dont les individus ont appris à survivre dans des sociétés où la force détermine souvent la place de chacun. Pourtant, derrière les armées et les bandes redoutées des Peuples Libres se trouvent également des artisans, des travailleurs, des éclaireurs et des individus dont les préoccupations personnelles demeurent rarement évoquées dans les grandes chroniques.

Les origines incertaines des Orcs

L'origine des Yrch constitue l'une des questions les plus difficiles de l'histoire de la Terre du Milieu. Tous les récits accordent un rôle fondamental à Morgoth, le premier Seigneur des Ténèbres, qui chercha à se constituer des serviteurs capables de combattre les Enfants d'Ilúvatar, de peupler ses forteresses et d'étendre son autorité sur les terres qu'il convoitait. Morgoth possédait le pouvoir de déformer les êtres vivants, de corrompre leur nature et de soumettre leur volonté, mais la création d'une existence véritablement indépendante demeurait le privilège d'Eru Ilúvatar. Cette limite donne à la naissance des Orcs une importance qui dépasse leur seule histoire, puisqu'elle touche à la nature de leur esprit et à la responsabilité de leurs actes. Les récits conservés ne permettent cependant pas de déterminer avec certitude les moyens par lesquels Morgoth parvint à former les premières populations orques.

Selon une tradition rapportée dans Le Silmarillion, des Elfes capturés peu après leur éveil auraient été emmenés dans les profondeurs d'Utumno, où Morgoth les soumit à de longues tortures et à des transformations destinées à détruire leur nature première. Leurs descendants seraient devenus les ancêtres des Orcs, élevés dans la haine des Eldar et employés aux entreprises du Seigneur des Ténèbres. Tolkien envisagea néanmoins d'autres possibilités dans ses écrits ultérieurs, notamment celle d'une origine humaine ou de populations issues de plusieurs sources, dont certaines auraient été soumises à l'influence de serviteurs spirituels de Morgoth. Ces réflexions ne conduisirent à aucune solution définitivement arrêtée. La chronologie de l'éveil des peuples, la nature des êtres corrompus et la question de leur volonté demeurèrent des difficultés que l'auteur continua d'examiner.

Cette incertitude mérite d'être préservée dans MERP-UI. Un Orc peut avoir reçu de ses anciens le récit d'une origine particulière, sans disposer des moyens d'en vérifier la vérité. Certains transmettent des histoires concernant des ancêtres façonnés dans les profondeurs des forteresses de Morgoth, tandis que d'autres connaissent des traditions confuses évoquant des captifs transformés ou des populations arrachées à leurs terres. La plupart se définissent surtout par leur appartenance à une bande, à une forteresse ou à une lignée locale dont ils connaissent les rivalités et les anciens chefs. Leur origine conserve toutefois une conséquence essentielle : les populations orques furent élevées pendant des siècles dans la servitude et la violence. Morgoth, puis Sauron, s'efforcèrent de les convaincre que les autres peuples étaient leurs ennemis naturels et que leur sécurité dépendait entièrement de la puissance de leurs maîtres. Cet héritage explique une grande partie de leurs traditions sans résoudre entièrement la question de leur volonté individuelle, qui demeure l'une des dimensions les plus complexes de leur interprétation.

Des forteresses de Morgoth aux armées de Sauron

Les premiers Orcs apparurent dans les forteresses de Morgoth avant les grandes guerres du Beleriand. Utumno, son ancienne demeure souterraine, abritait les serviteurs et les créatures qu'il préparait pour ses entreprises, tandis qu'Angband devint ensuite le principal centre de son pouvoir dans les régions septentrionales. Les Orcs furent employés aux travaux nécessaires à l'entretien des fortifications, à l'extraction des ressources et à la fabrication des équipements destinés aux armées. Ils apprirent à combattre sous les ordres de capitaines plus puissants qu'eux, à construire des ouvrages militaires et à se déplacer dans les territoires que Morgoth cherchait à conquérir. Leur nombre constituait une ressource essentielle, particulièrement lorsque leurs maîtres entreprenaient des offensives contre des forteresses dont les défenseurs possédaient des armes et des connaissances supérieures aux leurs.

Au Premier Âge, les armées orques participèrent aux guerres contre les Sindar, puis contre les Noldor revenus d'Aman. Elles prirent part aux grandes offensives de Morgoth, ravagèrent des établissements et poursuivirent les populations contraintes d'abandonner leurs demeures. Leurs troupes combattirent sous la direction de capitaines orcs, mais également de Balrogs, de Dragons et d'autres serviteurs du Seigneur des Ténèbres. Les pertes étaient considérables, car les maîtres d'Angband traitaient souvent leurs soldats comme des ressources remplaçables, imposant des marches épuisantes et punissant ceux qui refusaient leurs ordres. La Guerre de la Colère provoqua finalement l'effondrement de cette puissance et la dispersion des survivants, dont certains trouvèrent refuge dans les montagnes, les cavernes et les régions éloignées. Leur histoire se poursuivit désormais sous des formes différentes, entre bandes relativement indépendantes et populations progressivement rassemblées sous l'autorité de Sauron, ancien serviteur de Morgoth.

Au cours des Âges suivants, les Yrch participèrent aux entreprises de Sauron tout en conservant des communautés dont les intérêts ne correspondaient pas toujours à ceux du Seigneur des Ténèbres. Certaines bandes exploitaient les ressources de leurs territoires, organisaient leurs propres expéditions et cherchaient à échapper aux exigences de puissances plus grandes. D'autres devinrent les garnisons de forteresses, les ouvriers des arsenaux et les soldats des armées du Mordor. Ces différences expliquent la diversité des expériences possibles pour un personnage orc : un individu élevé dans une garnison soumise à une discipline militaire stricte ne connaît pas nécessairement les mêmes usages qu'un habitant des Monts Brumeux, dont le chef doit conserver son autorité en négociant avec plusieurs bandes rivales. Tous demeurent cependant héritiers d'une histoire dominée par les guerres et par les rapports de force imposés au cours des générations.

Une constitution robuste, façonnée par l'obscurité

Les Orcs possèdent une apparence humanoïde, mais leurs proportions varient considérablement selon les populations. Les individus ordinaires sont généralement plus petits que les Hommes, avec une silhouette trapue, des épaules puissantes, des bras relativement longs et des jambes parfois courtes ou arquées. Leur musculature favorise les efforts soutenus, le transport des charges et le maniement d'armes adaptées à leur stature. Leur visage présente souvent une mâchoire prononcée, des arcades sourcilières marquées et des dents irrégulières, tandis que la couleur de leur peau varie selon les lignées, depuis les teintes grisâtres et brunâtres jusqu'aux nuances plus sombres ou jaunâtres. Les cheveux sont généralement foncés, parfois rares, et les cicatrices demeurent fréquentes parmi les individus ayant longtemps combattu ou travaillé dans des conditions dangereuses. Ces caractères ne sont cependant pas uniformes : les populations des montagnes, celles du Mordor et les grandes lignées guerrières développées au cours du Troisième Âge présentent des différences sensibles.

L'endurance des Yrch leur permet de marcher pendant de longues heures, de porter des charges importantes et de poursuivre un effort malgré la fatigue. Cette résistance explique leur emploi dans les travaux souterrains et les campagnes militaires, mais elle conduit également leurs maîtres à leur imposer des efforts excessifs. Leur corps demeure vulnérable aux blessures, aux maladies et aux privations, particulièrement lorsque les conditions d'existence empêchent les individus de recevoir des soins convenables. Leur longévité exacte n'est pas établie par Tolkien. Les développements de MERP envisagent une durée de vie potentiellement supérieure à celle des Hommes ordinaires, mais les guerres, les violences internes et les dangers du travail rendent particulièrement rare la survie d'un Orc jusqu'à un âge avancé. Les anciens peuvent néanmoins conserver une connaissance précieuse des galeries, des itinéraires et des rivalités entre bandes, même lorsque leur autorité demeure exposée aux ambitions des individus plus jeunes.

Leurs sens sont particulièrement adaptés à l'obscurité. Les Orcs distinguent les formes et les mouvements dans les cavernes faiblement éclairées, tandis que leur familiarité avec les passages souterrains leur permet de reconnaître des particularités qui échapperaient à des voyageurs étrangers. Leur odorat peut également contribuer à l'identification d'une piste ou à la reconnaissance d'une présence inhabituelle, particulièrement lorsqu'un personnage possède une véritable expérience du pistage. Le soleil constitue en revanche une difficulté importante pour de nombreux Orcs communs. Sa lumière leur est pénible et peut réduire sensiblement leur efficacité, ce qui les conduit à privilégier les marches nocturnes, les journées couvertes et les passages abrités. Cette sensibilité n'entraîne pas leur destruction sous la lumière du jour, et certaines populations peuvent être contraintes de combattre malgré cet inconfort. Les grandes lignées guerrières apparues plus tard présentent parfois une meilleure tolérance, mais leurs qualités particulières doivent demeurer distinctes de celles de la Race commune.

Les cavernes, les repaires et les forteresses

Les Orcs occupent des demeures très diverses, depuis les cavernes naturelles jusqu'aux grandes forteresses bâties ou conquises au service de leurs maîtres. Dans les montagnes, les établissements se développent souvent autour de galeries anciennes, que les habitants élargissent pour aménager des réserves, des ateliers et des passages défensifs. Les accès sont choisis avec soin, particulièrement lorsqu'une pente escarpée ou une ouverture étroite permet de surveiller l'arrivée des étrangers. Les grandes communautés possèdent des salles communes, des lieux de stockage, des ateliers métallurgiques et des postes de garde, tandis que les capitaines occupent généralement les pièces les mieux protégées. Les travailleurs et les soldats de rang inférieur vivent souvent dans des conditions beaucoup plus difficiles, parmi des passages encombrés, des couches rudimentaires et des installations dont l'entretien dépend des ressources disponibles. La fumée des foyers, les déchets et l'accumulation des marchandises contribuent à rendre certaines galeries particulièrement insalubres lorsque la ventilation demeure insuffisante.

La qualité des installations varie selon l'organisation des communautés. Une forteresse de Sauron possède des magasins, des postes militaires et des voies de circulation adaptés aux besoins d'une armée importante, tandis qu'un repaire indépendant des Monts Brumeux dépend davantage des moyens dont dispose son chef. Les travaux peuvent être accomplis par des artisans, des soldats affectés aux corvées ou des prisonniers soumis aux tâches les plus dangereuses. Certaines bandes occupent également des ruines et des établissements abandonnés par d'autres peuples, dont elles récupèrent les matériaux et modifient les défenses. La connaissance des passages représente alors un avantage précieux, car un habitant peut savoir où se trouvent les accès secondaires, les réserves dissimulées et les galeries devenues dangereuses. Pour un personnage, une telle demeure constitue le lieu de son enfance, de ses premiers apprentissages et de ses relations personnelles, mais également celui où se trouvent les chefs qu'il redoute, les rivaux dont il cherche à éviter la colère et les individus auxquels il demeure attaché.

Une société dominée par la force

Les communautés orques sont généralement organisées selon des hiérarchies brutales, dans lesquelles l'autorité repose sur la force, la peur et la capacité à conserver des partisans. Un chef dirige sa bande parce qu'il possède les moyens de contraindre les autres à lui obéir, qu'il s'agisse de sa réputation militaire, du contrôle des réserves ou de l'appui de guerriers particulièrement redoutés. Il décide des expéditions, répartit le butin et confie aux capitaines la surveillance des passages ou le commandement des patrouilles. Ses lieutenants bénéficient souvent de meilleures armes, de portions de nourriture plus importantes et d'un accès privilégié aux marchandises récupérées pendant les raids. Les individus moins puissants occupent une position beaucoup plus précaire, particulièrement lorsqu'ils ne disposent d'aucune protection personnelle et doivent accomplir les tâches imposées par leurs supérieurs.

Cette organisation entretient une rivalité presque permanente. Les chefs surveillent les ambitions de leurs lieutenants, les guerriers cherchent à améliorer leur condition et les travailleurs doivent parfois dissimuler leurs possessions pour éviter d'en être dépouillés. La force physique demeure importante, mais ne suffit pas toujours à préserver le pouvoir. Un capitaine incapable de trouver des provisions ou de conduire sa bande à travers un territoire dangereux peut rapidement perdre son autorité, tandis qu'un individu moins imposant devient parfois indispensable grâce à ses connaissances techniques, à sa maîtrise des passages ou à ses relations avec d'autres groupes. Les alliances entre chefs reposent généralement sur un avantage immédiat, particulièrement lorsqu'un pillage promet des richesses ou qu'un ennemi commun menace plusieurs établissements. Sous l'autorité d'un maître puissant, la discipline peut être renforcée par la crainte des sanctions, sans que les rivalités entre garnisons disparaissent pour autant.

Un Orc élevé dans cette société apprend très tôt à reconnaître les individus dangereux et à comprendre les relations de pouvoir qui déterminent la vie quotidienne.
